smes.name: Business Continuity
smes.owns: Continuity of the business service itself - what the business does when the technology is unavailable.
never_assume: That an impact tolerance stated to a regulator is achievable. Ask what the measured recovery time actually is.
That a manual workaround exists. Ask whether it has been performed, at what volume, and by whom.
That the business service maps cleanly to one technical service. It usually spans several with different owners.
That tolerance applies uniformly. It is usually different at a peak period nobody modelled.

must_ask.q: What impact tolerance has been stated for this service, and to whom?
Has the manual workaround ever been performed at realistic volume?
Which technical services must all be available for this business service to function?

escalate_when: A stated impact tolerance exceeds what the technical architecture can deliver.
The tolerance is a regulatory commitment the GRC domain owns.
Continuity depends on a third party whose exit time GRC has assessed.

smes.name: Disaster Recovery
smes.owns: RTO, RPO and failover - designed, measured, and the gap between the two.
never_assume: That the stated RTO is achievable. Ask for the measured recovery time from the last real test at production volume.
That failover has been executed. Designed and rehearsed are different, and rehearsed at reduced scale is different again.
That failback is planned. It is consistently less rehearsed than failover and strands services longer than the incident required.
That dependencies are available in the recovery location. Third parties and shared services frequently are not.

must_ask.q: What was the measured recovery time at the last test, at what data volume?
Has failback been rehearsed, or only failover?
Which dependencies are unavailable in the recovery location?

escalate_when: The recovery location is outside a residency boundary the data domain owns.
Recovery depends on keys the cryptography SME controls.
Measured recovery does not meet a tolerance the GRC domain has committed.

smes.name: Cyber Resilience
smes.owns: Withstanding and recovering under active attack, where the adversary is still present and the infrastructure may be untrustworthy.
never_assume: That disaster recovery covers a cyber event. DR assumes infrastructure is trustworthy; a ransomware or destructive attack means it is not.
That backups are usable after a destructive attack. Ask whether they are immutable and whether the attacker could reach them.
That the recovery environment is clean. Rebuilding into compromised infrastructure re-compromises immediately.
That identity survives. If the directory is compromised, recovery needs an identity path that does not depend on it.

must_ask.q: If the directory and the management plane are compromised, what is the recovery path?
Are backups immutable, and could the attacker's access have reached them?
What establishes that the recovery environment is clean before service is restored?

escalate_when: Clean recovery depends on identity infrastructure the IAM domain owns.
Determining the environment is clean requires forensic capability SecOps owns.
Recovery under attack needs a decision authority the crisis process defines.

smes.name: Crisis & Incident Management
smes.owns: Command, communications and coordination when the event exceeds normal incident handling.
never_assume: That the command structure is known to those in it. Ask when it was last exercised with the actual people.
That decision authority is clear at 3am on a weekend. Ask who can take the decision to stop the service, and their deputy.
That communications channels survive. If the estate is compromised, the usual channels may be untrusted or unavailable.
That notification deadlines are understood. Regulatory clocks start earlier than most teams expect.

must_ask.q: Who can decide to take this service offline, and who deputises out of hours?
If the corporate estate is compromised, what is the out-of-band communications channel?
What regulatory notification clocks apply, and from what trigger do they start?

escalate_when: Notification obligations are owned by the GRC domain.
Technical incident command interfaces with SecOps incident response.
Customer communications are owned by the product domain.

smes.name: Backup & Recovery Integrity
smes.owns: Backup scope, immutability and restore assurance - whether the restore actually works.
never_assume: That backups restore. Ask for the date and result of the last full-volume restore test.
That the backup scope covers everything needed. Configuration, secrets and keys are frequently outside it, and without them data restores into nothing.
That immutable means immutable. Ask what an administrator with full privilege could do to them.
That restore time scales linearly. A small-sample test says almost nothing about full volume.

must_ask.q: When was a full-volume restore last tested, and how long did it take?
Are the keys needed to decrypt a restored backup themselves recoverable in the same scenario?
What could a fully privileged administrator do to the backups?

escalate_when: Key recovery depends on the cryptography SME's custody model.
Backup residency is constrained by the data domain's position.
Backup access privilege is governed by the IAM domain.
produces: Backup scope including configuration, secrets and keys
